opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this in terms of levels, kind of like self-driving cars. Right now we're somewhere around level two or three. Agents can help you read the literature, generate hypotheses, write analysis code, and even design experiments. But the human is still very much in the driver's seat, deciding which ideas are worth pursuing and interpreting what comes back from the lab.

The real bottleneck to closing the loop isn't the reasoning side anymore. Language models are getting surprisingly good at the "thinking" part of science. The bottleneck is the physical world. Biology is wet, messy, and slow. You can run a million simulations in silico, but at some point you have to pipette something, grow cells, and wait for them to do their thing. Cells don't care how fast your GPU is.

So I think the progression goes something like this. First, agents become really good research assistants: literature synthesis, data analysis, protocol generation. That's largely happening now. Next, you connect them to lab automation, so an agent can propose an experiment, send it to robotic hardware or a cloud lab, get the data back, and decide what to do next. That's where things get exciting, because you can start running many iterations of design, build, test, learn without a human in every cycle.

The hard part is that most lab work today isn't automatable in a clean, API-driven way. There's a lot of tacit knowledge, the "hands" of an experienced postdoc. So part of the work is building the infrastructure, both the hardware and the data standards, so experiments become reproducible and machine-readable.

And then the last piece is taste. Knowing which questions actually matter is still deeply human. I don't think we fully close the loop until agents can judge not just whether an experiment worked, but whether it was worth doing. That's the frontier I find most interesting: getting from a virtual cell model that predicts outcomes to an AI scientist that knows what to ask in the first place.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this as a loop with a few distinct stages, and the question is really which stages are being closed and how fast.

The classic scientific method is: you read the literature, you form a hypothesis, you design an experiment, you run it, you analyze the data, and then you update your beliefs and go again. For a long time the AI story in biology was really just the analysis step. You'd get a model that's good at protein structure or at reading sequencing data, and that's genuinely useful, but it's one piece of the loop. The human is still doing all the thinking about what to do next.

What's changed in the last couple of years is that the models have gotten good enough at reasoning and at reading the literature that they can start to do the hypothesis generation and the experimental design parts. That's the part I find most exciting, honestly, because that's where the taste lives. A good scientist isn't someone who runs a lot of experiments, it's someone who picks the right experiment. And we're starting to see agents that can look at a body of evidence, notice a gap, and propose something that's actually non-obvious.

The hard part, and where I think most of the work is right now, is the physical execution step. In silico you can close the loop pretty completely, you can have an agent propose a model, train it, evaluate it, and iterate, and that's already happening. But biology is wet. You have to actually grow the cells, do the edits, run the assay. So closing the loop means you need lab automation that an agent can drive, and you need the agent to be able to interpret messy, noisy experimental results, including when the experiment just failed for a boring reason.

So my view is that it's going to come in layers. First you get agents that are really strong research assistants, they do the literature synthesis and the analysis and they suggest experiments, and the human is the one who presses go. Then you get agents that can run end-to-end in computational domains where the whole loop is in software. And then, as the automated lab infrastructure matures, you get the fully closed loop in the wet lab, where the agent is proposing, executing, measuring, and iterating, maybe running hundreds of these cycles in parallel.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking the bottleneck is purely the AI. A lot of it is the plumbing. Can your instruments talk to each other? Is your data structured in a way a model can actually learn from? Those are unglamorous problems but they're what gates the whole thing. The groups that get there first are going to be the ones that treat the lab itself as a system you design for agents, not just a place where you put a model on top of what humans were already doing.

astra-6.text:
I think the key transition is from AI that helps you think about an experiment to AI that can learn from doing one. An agent can propose a hypothesis, design an experiment, and analyze results, but closing the loop means connecting those steps to actual experimental execution—and then letting the results change what it does next.

The hard part is that science doesn’t give you a clean reward signal. If an experiment fails, was the hypothesis wrong? Was the assay unreliable? Did something go wrong with the execution? An effective scientific agent needs to reason about that uncertainty and choose experiments that distinguish between those possibilities.

So I’d expect this to happen first in bounded settings, where you have reliable measurements, relatively fast experiments, and enough automation to iterate. Then the scope expands as those systems become more dependable. The really interesting milestone is when a system produces a surprising result, follows it up with the right controls, and establishes something reproducible. That’s a much stronger demonstration of scientific discovery than generating a plausible hypothesis.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll get there in stages. Today, agents can already help with pieces of the process: reading papers, generating hypotheses, writing code, and analyzing results. The next step is connecting those capabilities to experiments, so an agent can propose a test, execute it, look at the data, and decide what to do next.

The critical part is that feedback loop. Coming up with a plausible hypothesis is very different from making a prediction that survives contact with an experiment. A useful scientific agent needs to recognize when an experiment failed, when its hypothesis was wrong, and when the measurement itself is unreliable.

I’d expect this to work first in relatively constrained settings where experiments are fast and the results are easy to measure. As those systems become more reliable, we can move toward longer, more complex research programs. Humans will still have an important role in choosing worthwhile questions and setting constraints, but agents could dramatically increase how many ideas we can actually test.
